tagline.text: Pampanga's Good Friday Passion rites, with a Calvary raised in the rice fields

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay San Pedro Cutud, San Fernando, Pampanga

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Good Friday (March–April; the date changes every year)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~2,000 (day trip from Manila; transport, food and drink, estimated)

children.text: Every Good Friday, the barangay of San Pedro Cutud in San Fernando, Pampanga, stages a passion play and a re-enactment of the crucifixion in which penitents are nailed to crosses. It is the highlight of Maleldo (Holy Week), and thousands of locals and foreign visitors gather. The Catholic Church does not encourage the practice, so please learn the cultural context and watch from a respectful distance.

The San Pedro Cutud Lenten Rites take place on Good Friday in Barangay San Pedro Cutud in San Fernando, the capital of Pampanga. They are the highlight of "Maleldo," the Kapampangan word for Holy Week: a passion play re-enacting the suffering and death of Jesus is followed by the nailing of a few penitents to wooden crosses. The setting is a makeshift "Calvary" built in the village rice fields, which Wikipedia describes as about
3 km
from the San Fernando town proper (poblacion).

The roots of the event lie in a modest Via Crucis (Way of the Cross) play staged by amateur village volunteers in 1955. It is known as the only Passion play written in Kapampangan. The first actual crucifixion during the play came in 1962, when Artemio Anoza, a self-styled doctor from nearby Apalit, was nailed to a cross, an event that drew national and international media attention, according to local reports. The rites have continued every year since and have become one of the best-known Holy Week events in the Philippines; they are also listed in the Philippine Intangible Cultural Heritage inventory (Pinagmulan) compiled by the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA).

The people who are nailed to the cross do so to seek atonement, to pray for the sick, to give thanks for miracles, or to keep a yearly vow. The best-known figure is Ruben Enaje, called the "Christ of Pampanga." A painter, he first took the cross in thanks for surviving a fall from a three-story building, and the Daily Tribune reported that on Good Friday 2026, at age 65, he went through his 37th year of penance. He had said in 2025 that it would be his last, yet he returned the following year; he has not yet decided whether he will come back next year.

Please understand first that this is an act of faith by villagers, not a tourist show. The Catholic Church in the Philippines does not encourage this kind of self-inflicted penance and has urged people to express their faith through prayer, sincere repentance and charity such as blood donation. A 2018 report explains that the San Fernando city government is not a participant in the rites; the host barangays run them directly, and the city only keeps the peace and looks after participants' health. Even so, thousands come every year, so it is best to attend as a quiet witness rather than as a spectator.

blocks.title: Passion play of the Way of the Cross

children.text: A play in Kapampangan re-enacting the trial and the walk to the cross forms the backbone of the event. Villagers dressed as Roman soldiers perform it, and it is the original form of the event that has continued since 1955.

blocks.title: Calvary in the middle of the rice fields

children.text: A temporary hill with crosses is set up in a village rice field. The row of crosses, the paddies stretching behind them and the crowd gathered around make a scene that is hard to find elsewhere.

The penitents' palms are fixed to the cross with stainless steel nails about 2 inches long, disinfected by soaking in alcohol, while ropes and cloth support the body. Wikipedia explains that penitents are taken down once they feel their sins have been cleansed.
Penitents called magdarame carry wooden crosses through the streets and whip their own backs with bamboo sticks called burilyos. You can see this on the village roads before the nailing.
Besides San Pedro Cutud, similar rites are held in San Juan and Santa Lucia in San Fernando. In the 2026 San Fernando city schedule, crucifixions were set for about
in San Juan,
in Santa Lucia and
in Cutud (a 2018 report gave 6:00, 9:00 and 10:00). Times change every year, so check the current schedule locally.

In 2026 it was also reported that a senakulo (Passion play) was held on Good Friday morning in Barangay Calulut. Even if you do not watch the crucifixions, you can experience local Holy Week faith culture.

Besides Enaje, there are others such as Wilfredo Salvador of Barangay San Juan (in his 18th year in 2026), who continued the penance after recovering from an illness, and others who carry on a tradition begun by their fathers. Their stories are told in news reports.

The rites are listed in the Philippine Intangible Cultural Heritage inventory and have been mentioned as a possible candidate for UNESCO lists. In other words, they are regarded as both a religious observance and a folk tradition.

items.title: Good Friday itinerary
items.subtitle: From early arrival to the afternoon wrap-up

children.text: If you start from Manila, set out in the early dawn. On Good Friday the roads north can be congested and San Fernando itself can get crowded.
Arrive in downtown San Fernando, have breakfast and pick up water and a hat. The venue is about
3 km
from the town center, so go by tricycle or on foot.
Enter Cutud village and choose your spot. People start gathering in the morning, so arriving early to find shade and a good view is the best approach.
Watch the magdarame procession and the first part of the passion play. Penitents carrying crosses pass along the street while the crowd gathers on both sides.
The crucifixion takes place at the Calvary. In the 2026 city schedule it began at about
(10:00 AM in 2018), but this can differ from year to year, so check local announcements.
Leave before the crowd disperses after the event, then have lunch and rest. The midday heat is intense, so do not push yourself.
Visit a church in town or a nearby sight, then head back while avoiding the peak return-traffic hours.
The exact Good Friday schedule is announced each year by the city and the village. This itinerary is only an example based on past reports, so check the latest announcements.

items.title: Two-day Holy Week itinerary
items.subtitle: Exploring Pampanga on Maundy Thursday + Good Friday

children.text: Arrive in Clark or San Fernando on Maundy Thursday afternoon and check in. This reduces how early you must travel on Good Friday.
Explore downtown San Fernando and nearby heritage sites such as Bacolor Church. During Holy Week, penitents sometimes appear along the roadside.
Have dinner with Pampanga cuisine and rest early, since you need to move at dawn on Good Friday.
Leave your lodging early on Good Friday and head to Cutud. The early crucifixions in San Juan village need to be checked separately.
Watch the passion play and the crucifixion in Cutud.
After lunch, continue to nearby plans such as Clark or Mount Arayat, or return to Manila.
Shops and public transport may be reduced on Good Friday, so find out about your return transport in advance.
San Fernando is about
north of Manila (Wikipedia says 66 km; the San Fernando city government profile says 67 km).
Take a bus bound for Pampanga or San Fernando from a bus terminal in Manila and get off in San Fernando. Check the Good Friday schedule and fares locally.
From downtown San Fernando to the venue, go by tricycle or on foot.
Traffic can be heavy on Good Friday, so leave early.
San Fernando is about
south of Clark (Angeles) (city government profile 16 km, Wikipedia 17 km).
If you arrive at Clark International Airport (CRK), you can reach San Fernando by Grab, taxi or bus. Check Holy Week fares and waiting times locally.
According to a 2013 visitor's account, you take a jeepney from San Fernando toward the Provincial Capitol, then walk or take a tricycle; the venue was about
1–2 km
away (a 2017 account says it was a couple of kilometres on foot from the barangay entrance, so allow extra time).
On the day, nearby roads may be closed or congested, so be prepared to get off where you can and walk.
Parking is difficult if you drive, so public transport is recommended.

The rites are held only on Good Friday, the Friday before Easter, so the date changes every year. In recent reports it was April 18 in 2025 and April 3 in 2026. Check an Easter calendar for future dates.

Good Friday falls at the tail end of the Philippine dry season, and the midday heat is fierce. In 2026, too, people fainted under the blazing sun and were treated by medical teams. Arrive early in the morning if you can and plan ways to avoid the sun.

You can stay in downtown San Fernando or in nearby Clark (Angeles). Rooms fill quickly during Holy Week, so book early. A day trip from Manila is possible but requires an early start.

Pampanga is known as the culinary capital of the Philippines. Shops may have reduced hours on Good Friday, so check whether restaurants are open. A 2026 report says stalls around the venue sold water and snacks and did decent business. Please choose establishments on the spot.
Arrive early on Good Friday to secure shade and a good view.
Bring plenty of water and prepare a hat and sunscreen. It is hot enough that people faint at midday.
Do not get close with a phone or camera in a way that disturbs the penitents or the organizers; keep a respectful distance.
Dress lightly but neatly, which suits a religious event.
There are accounts that access for media may be limited, so follow local guidance on whether photography is allowed.
Guard against pickpockets by keeping valuables close and wearing your bag in front in the crowd.
Decide your return transport and time in advance. Roads clog around the time the event ends.
Besides the crucifixions, watching the area's non-violent Holy Week events (plays and processions) will give you a broader understanding of the culture.
This is a self-inflicted penance that the Catholic Church does not encourage, and it includes actual nailing. The scenes can be shocking, and the crowd and heat can be dangerous, so do not overdo it.

Whether the event is held and its schedule can change from year to year. During the pandemic the village blocked the crucifixions and they were not held for several years, so check the latest announcements.
In 2026 the crowd was larger than expected and some people collapsed from the heat. If you are frail or traveling with young children, think carefully.
Do not approach, touch or block the penitents. Follow the control of on-site staff and the police.
Watch out for theft and getting separated, and agree on a meeting place with your group in the crowd.
The participants are people acting out of faith. Do not mock them or take disrespectful photos.
